content: 1. Health-care facilities should assess the type of exposure experienced by health and care workers who have been exposed to Ebola or Marburg viruses at work. 2. A process should be implemented to monitor the health of exposed workers for the development of symptoms. 3. If laboratory resources are available, testing of exposed workers should be considered to potentially shorten the exclusion period from work. 4. Excluded health and care workers should be compensated for their time away from work. 5. Community and worker sensitization and engagement should be offered to reduce stigma associated with exclusion. 6. The impact of exclusion on equity should be assessed, as the situation may evolve dynamically during an outbreak, potentially affecting the number of workers excluded. 7. The decision to exclude exposed workers should remain flexible to adapt to the changing circumstances of an outbreak and operational considerations for health service delivery. 8. The exclusion period for health workers should be 21 days from the last known exposure to Ebola or Marburg viruses. For example, if the last exposure occurred on January 1, the exclusion period would end on January 22, and the worker could return to work on January 23. 9. If symptoms develop during the exclusion period, the worker should undergo a full medical assessment, ideally at a treatment center, and their exclusion period should be extended if they are found to be infected. 10. Excluded workers should self-quarantine and be monitored daily. 11. Exposed workers should receive instructions on self-monitoring for signs and symptoms of Ebola or Marburg disease for 21 days post-exposure and should seek immediate medical attention if symptoms develop. 12. Vaccination should be offered to health workers who have not been previously vaccinated, in accordance with current guidelines. 13. The WHO suggests that health and care workers exposed to Ebola or Marburg viruses be excluded from work for 21 days. 14. Exclusion is more likely to be adopted when the worker has not been vaccinated within the recommended timeframe, the exposure is assessed as high-risk, adequate staffing is available to maintain health services, and there is a low risk of stigma for the worker. 15. The systematic review did not identify evidence of the effects of exclusion versus non-exclusion on health worker infections or health-care-associated transmission of Ebola or Marburg viruses. 16. The primary goal of excluding exposed workers is to prevent onward transmission to other staff or patients. However, vaccination status and the risk level of the exposure may influence this decision. 17. Exclusion may lead to reduced staffing levels and challenges in maintaining health services, which could negatively impact the health system. 18. Some health workers may face stigma within their communities if excluded from work. 19. Excluded workers may not receive pay for their time off, which could have financial consequences for them. 20. The benefits of exclusion are considered small, and the harms are variable depending on the context. On balance, the WHO likely favors not excluding health workers from work. 21. Ebola and Marburg viruses have similar environmental survivability, so disinfection practices can be applied to both. 22. Ebola virus can survive for up to 15 days on nonporous surfaces in low-humidity, 22°C conditions. 23. The virus survives longer in low-humidity, low-temperature settings, which are generally different from African settings. 24. Ebola virus can survive in wastewater, but viable concentrations diminish rapidly after 24 hours, with recovery possible for up to eight days. Standard chlorine levels used for water disinfection inactivate the virus in wastewater. 25. The virus can survive for up to 16 days in dried blood on nonporous surfaces. 26. In real-world studies, Ebola virus RNA has been found only on visibly soiled surfaces and in the immediate vicinity of patients. Disinfection practices are generally effective in these cases. 27. Six studies reported environmental audits of highand low-risk surfaces in Ebola treatment units, finding viral RNA primarily in areas near patients or on visibly soiled surfaces. 28. Current disinfection protocols are effective, but discrepancies between experimental and real-world findings highlight the need for further high-quality research. 29. A 0.5% hypochlorite solution (1000 ppm available chlorine) is effective for surface disinfection. 30. On nonporous, contaminated surfaces without visible spills, 10 minutes of contact time is consistently effective. 31. For visibly soiled surfaces, cleaning followed by disinfection is recommended. 32. The use of peracetic acid on dried spills should be considered but requires further investigation. 33. Cleaning and disinfection should occur immediately after patient discharge or when surfaces are visibly contaminated with blood or body fluids. 34. Spraying disinfectants in areas with patients present is not advised, as it may not always be feasible to remove all patients from the location. 35. Non-porous surfaces are recommended in health-care settings to facilitate effective cleaning and disinfection. 36. Organic material should be removed prior to disinfection to reduce the organic load. 37. Disinfection of areas with no direct contact with patients or body fluids, such as certain ambulance surfaces, may be a lower priority or unnecessary. 38. Dead-body management is not covered in this recommendation but is addressed in a separate section on the safe management of dead bodies. 39. The WHO emphasizes the need for further research to address gaps in evidence, such as the impact of vaccination as post-exposure prophylaxis and the feasibility of excluding health workers based on exposure risk. 40. Research protocols, including data collection tools, are needed to evaluate these gaps. 41. The ability to exclude health workers depends on the availability of replacement staff and the capacity to pay excluded workers. 42. Work exclusion is considered probably feasible, but its implementation will depend on the specific context and resources available.
